messages.content: I want to develop domain-generalization methods that can distinguish transferable predictive features from spurious features, without source-domain annotations or target-domain data.

The aim is to retain features that genuinely help prediction across domains while avoiding dependence on features whose apparent usefulness comes from spurious correlations. The two information constraints matter: the method cannot rely on labels identifying which source domain an example came from, and it cannot rely on data from the target domain.
I also want a concrete performance target: at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under unseen combinations of spurious correlations.

That sets ERM as the comparison baseline and worst-domain accuracy as the measure for that requirement. The gain must be at least 5 percentage points—not a 5 percent relative increase—and it must hold when the spurious correlations appear in combinations not seen before.
Why emphasize the worst domain rather than just overall accuracy?

Worst-domain accuracy focuses on the domain where performance is lowest. An overall average could look favorable while masking a substantial failure on one domain. Your target asks whether the method improves that weakest outcome relative to ERM under the specified unseen combinations.
I don't want that improvement to come from sacrificing performance on the sources.

There is a second requirement: average source-domain accuracy must stay within one percentage point of ERM. The goal therefore combines a gain in worst-domain accuracy with close-to-ERM average accuracy on the source domains, rather than treating either measure alone as sufficient.
Does “within one percentage point” mean the same kind of comparison as the five-point target?

Both are expressed in percentage points, but they serve different purposes. The worst-domain requirement calls for an improvement of at least 5 points over ERM; the source-domain requirement calls for the average to remain within 1 point of ERM. For a purely illustrative reading, if ERM's average source-domain accuracy were 80%, an average of 79% would be one percentage point away. That example does not specify an actual result.
How should I describe what counts as a spurious feature here?

Conceptually, a spurious feature may be predictive because of a correlation that does not reliably carry over to the domains of interest. A transferable predictive feature is useful in a way that can persist across domains. The goal is to distinguish those roles without assuming that the distinction has already been identified for any particular feature.
And preserving genuinely predictive features is an explicit part of the goal, not just a side effect?

Yes. The requirement is not simply to suppress anything associated with a source domain or to discard as much information as possible. It is to resist spurious correlations while preserving features that genuinely support prediction. That preservation matters alongside both accuracy comparisons.
Could a feature be useful on the sources and still be spurious for this purpose?

Yes, in the general sense intended by the goal. A feature can correlate with the outcome in available source data yet fail to remain useful when the correlation changes. Source usefulness by itself does not settle whether a feature is transferable; that is the distinction the proposed methods are meant to address.
Does the lack of source-domain annotations mean there are no source examples or no prediction labels?

No. It specifically says source-domain annotations are unavailable: the method is not given identifiers saying which source domain each example belongs to. It does not, by itself, say that source examples or their prediction labels are unavailable. The phrase “average source-domain accuracy” describes a performance requirement, not permission for the method to use source-domain identifiers.
What does the absence of target-domain data rule out in the statement of the goal?

It rules out relying on observations from the target domain to distinguish features or make the method work. The desired generalization must address domains not supplied as target-domain data to the method. Assessing accuracy on an unseen domain is conceptually different from giving that domain's data to the method as an input.
I want to be precise about “unseen combinations of spurious correlations.” Is that stronger than discussing a single spurious correlation in isolation?

It specifies the setting for the worst-domain comparison: combinations of spurious correlations that have not been seen before. The requirement is not limited to a case where only one spurious correlation differs at a time. It does not, however, specify which correlations or combinations will occur.
Can we say yet that a particular way of separating features will achieve this?

No particular method or result is stated. This is a development goal with performance requirements, not a completed experiment or a claim that the separation has already been achieved. Any proposed method would need to be assessed against the stated constraints and comparisons.
So the two accuracy requirements should be read together?

Yes. The intended method should achieve at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under unseen combinations of spurious correlations, while keeping average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. It must do so without source-domain annotations or target-domain data, and without losing genuinely predictive features merely to reduce reliance on spurious ones.
Would it misstate the aim to say that all features correlated with a source prediction should be removed?

It would. Correlation with a prediction is not, on its own, what makes a feature spurious. The aim is to tell apart genuinely transferable predictive information and misleading, nontransferable associations. Indiscriminate removal could discard the very predictive features the goal says to preserve.
Then how cautiously should I phrase the ambition?

As a target rather than an established outcome: develop methods that make that distinction under the stated data constraints, with a worst-domain gain of at least 5 percentage points over ERM in the specified unseen-correlation setting and average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. That wording preserves both the ambition and the fact that no result has been reported.
For that goal, I propose training SwapAnchor by exchanging inferred nuisance codes across labels, enforcing counterfactual consistency, and distilling ERM on original examples.

SwapAnchor is a proposed way to address the feature-separation goal, not a reported result. Its three stated parts have different roles: nuisance-code exchanges create the counterfactual changes of interest, consistency encourages predictions to withstand those changes, and ERM distillation on original examples provides a reference for retaining predictive behavior there.
What does “inferred nuisance codes” commit us to?

It says the codes are inferred rather than supplied as known descriptions of nuisance factors. Calling them nuisance codes expresses their intended role in the proposal; it does not establish that they isolate only spurious information. The proposal does not specify how they are inferred or what form they take.
And “across labels” is an important qualification to the exchange?

Yes. The proposed exchange is across labels, rather than merely rearranging codes among examples with the same label. It probes whether a prediction can remain grounded in the original example’s predictive information when the inferred nuisance component comes from a differently labeled example. That is the intended conceptual test, not proof that every exchange produces a valid counterfactual.
Could you unpack “counterfactual consistency” without assuming a particular model architecture?

At this level, it means encouraging a prediction to remain appropriately consistent when the inferred nuisance code is changed while the predictive identity being tested is meant to remain fixed. The statement does not prescribe a representation, a loss formula, or a way to construct the exchanged example. Those would be further design choices, not details already specified by the proposal.
So the consistency condition is meant to discourage dependence on whatever varies in the swap?

That is the intended pressure. If a change is genuinely confined to nuisance information, a label-relevant prediction should not need to follow it. The qualification matters: because the codes are inferred, the proposal alone cannot guarantee that a swap changes only nuisance information or that enforcing consistency always preserves the right distinctions.
Where does the ERM part enter? I specifically said distilling ERM on original examples.

That specifies both the reference and where distillation is applied: ERM is the model whose behavior is distilled, and the distillation is on original examples. It does not say to distill ERM’s predictions on the code-exchanged examples. Conceptually, the original-example term can anchor behavior while the consistency term addresses sensitivity to the proposed nuisance changes.
Is that anchor connected to the requirement to preserve genuinely predictive features and stay close to ERM on average source-domain accuracy?

It is a plausible motivation for including it. Distillation on original examples can be understood as a way to discourage the proposed method from abandoning useful predictive behavior while it learns consistency. But that mechanism alone does not establish that genuinely predictive features are preserved or that average source-domain accuracy stays within one percentage point of ERM; those remain requirements to assess.
Could matching ERM on original examples conflict with trying to avoid spurious correlations?

There is a conceptual tension: ERM behavior on original examples may reflect both useful predictive information and correlations the method aims not to rely on under change. The proposal combines original-example distillation with counterfactual consistency rather than claiming that ERM’s behavior is entirely transferable. How those pressures interact is not resolved by the proposal alone.
Does the swap itself identify which features are spurious?

Not automatically. It is a proposed way to expose sensitivity to information represented by the inferred nuisance codes. Whether those codes capture spurious features rather than genuinely predictive ones is a substantive question; the name of the codes and the consistency objective do not settle it.
I also don't want to imply that the method needs source-domain annotations to make these exchanges.

Nothing in the stated SwapAnchor proposal calls for source-domain annotations: the exchanges are described in terms of inferred codes and labels, not supplied domain identities. Likewise, it does not call for target-domain data. That makes the proposal compatible in its stated form with the goal’s information constraints, without specifying all the details needed to establish that a particular implementation obeys them.
How would you relate this proposal to the worst-domain target without claiming it has succeeded?

The intended connection is that reducing reliance on exchanged nuisance information might help when spurious correlations occur in unseen combinations. The actual target remains at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under those unseen combinations. SwapAnchor is a proposed route toward that target, not evidence that it reaches it.
Would better consistency on swaps, by itself, satisfy the goal?

No. Consistency is a training principle in the proposal, whereas the goal includes performance and preservation conditions. Even if the proposed consistency behavior were obtained, the method would still need to meet the worst-domain comparison, keep average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM, and preserve genuinely predictive features.
Can we say which nuisance codes to exchange, or how strongly to enforce the two training pressures?

Not from this proposal as stated. It names exchanges across labels, counterfactual consistency, and ERM distillation on original examples, but it does not specify code selection rules, a consistency metric, a distillation objective, or their relative strengths. Giving any of those a particular value or procedure would add a design decision.
Then I want a compact formulation that preserves the distinction between the proposal and its hoped-for outcome.

Propose SwapAnchor as a method that exchanges inferred nuisance codes across labels, enforces counterfactual consistency, and distills ERM on original examples. The intended purpose is to separate transferable predictive information from spurious reliance under the goal’s data constraints; whether it achieves the specified worst-domain improvement while preserving source accuracy and genuinely predictive features remains to be established.
How can SwapAnchor infer nuisance codes that are actually exchangeable without stripping away predictive structure when spurious cues co-occur with genuine features?

That is the central difficulty in the proposal. If an inferred code contains both a spurious cue and information genuinely needed for prediction, exchanging it may change more than a nuisance factor. Counterfactual consistency would then risk discouraging the model from using legitimate predictive information. SwapAnchor therefore needs a meaningful distinction between what may be exchanged and what must be preserved; calling a code “nuisance” does not establish that distinction.
What should “exchangeable” mean here? Is it enough that two codes can be swapped computationally?

No. A swap can be mechanically possible without being meaningful. For this question, exchangeability means that replacing the code can be interpreted as changing the nuisance aspect while leaving the predictive structure relevant to the original label intact. That is a substantive condition about what the representation captures, not just an operation the model can perform.
Why does co-occurrence of spurious and genuine features make that condition hard to establish?

Because the available observations may not cleanly separate their contributions. A cue can repeatedly appear alongside genuinely predictive information, so a code inferred from those observations may bundle both. If the code is then exchanged, a change in prediction does not, by itself, reveal whether the model was following the spurious cue or responding to predictive structure that the exchange also disturbed.
Does exchanging codes across labels resolve that ambiguity?

Not on its own. The across-label exchange is meant to probe reliance on the inferred nuisance component, but it depends on that component being sufficiently separate from label-relevant information. Taking a code from an example with another label does not guarantee that the resulting change is confined to a nuisance factor.
Then how can I discuss inference of these codes without pretending we already know which features are spurious?

Frame it as an inference problem with a necessary safeguard, rather than as an accomplished separation. The inferred codes would need to support exchanges that vary the suspected nuisance information without removing information needed for the original prediction. Whether they do so is precisely what is uncertain when spurious cues co-occur with genuine features.
What would go wrong if the inferred code captured part of the genuinely predictive signal?

An exchange could alter the basis on which the original label is predictable. Enforcing the same prediction after that exchange could then teach the model to ignore information it should retain. A model might appear insensitive to the swap while losing genuinely predictive distinctions—the opposite of the preservation requirement.
And what if the code fails to capture the spurious cue at all?

Then swapping it would not meaningfully challenge the model’s reliance on that cue. Consistency under those swaps could hold even while the model continues to use the spurious information. These are two different failure modes: moving predictive structure along with the code, and leaving the relevant nuisance information outside it.
So a stable prediction after a swap isn't automatically evidence that the code is well inferred?

Correct. Stability could be meaningful if the swap changed a nuisance factor while preserving the predictive structure. But stability alone cannot establish those conditions. The interpretation depends on what the exchange actually changes, not merely on whether a consistency objective is satisfied.
How does the ERM distillation on original examples bear on this particular concern?

It can provide pressure to retain predictive behavior on original examples, which is relevant to avoiding indiscriminate loss of information. It does not certify that the exchanged codes contain only nuisance information. Nor does agreement with ERM on original examples, by itself, show that predictive structure survives a code exchange.
Is there a circularity here—deciding a code is nuisance because predictions should stay fixed, then using fixed predictions to justify the code?

There can be if consistency is treated as the sole evidence of exchangeability. The intended counterfactual interpretation requires an independently meaningful reason to regard the exchanged component as nuisance rather than predictive. The question is how SwapAnchor can make that distinction when the observed cues are entangled; the consistency objective alone does not answer it.
Do the constraints on domain information make this harder to state?

They sharpen the question. The broader goal does not permit source-domain annotations or target-domain data as inputs to the method, so an account of nuisance-code inference cannot quietly assume either is available to identify what changes across domains. The issue remains whether the information available to SwapAnchor is sufficient to separate an exchangeable nuisance component from genuinely predictive structure.
Should I say that separation is impossible whenever the cues co-occur?

That would be stronger than the question supports. Co-occurrence makes the inference ambiguous and creates a risk of stripping predictive structure; it does not, by itself, establish an impossibility result for every setting. The appropriately cautious question is what would allow the inferred codes to be treated as exchangeable despite that entanglement.
Could we at least distinguish the property we want from the outcome we hope to achieve?

Yes. The property sought of the codes is that exchanging them changes nuisance information while preserving the predictive structure associated with the original example. The hoped-for outcome is that training on such exchanges helps SwapAnchor avoid spurious reliance without losing genuine predictive information. Neither the property nor the outcome follows just from naming the codes or performing swaps.
How would you state the unresolved issue in one direct question?

How can SwapAnchor infer codes whose across-label exchanges genuinely vary nuisance cues, rather than carrying away predictive structure, when those cues co-occur with genuine features? That keeps the focus on the validity of the inferred exchange, before treating counterfactual consistency as a reliable training signal.

I have a hypothesis for the exchangeability problem: within-class residual clustering after supervised bottlenecking isolates exchangeable nuisance codes, and ERM distillation limits source-accuracy loss to at most 1 percentage point.

That is a proposed answer to how SwapAnchor might infer nuisance codes without stripping predictive structure. The first part hypothesizes that a supervised bottleneck retains information needed for prediction, leaving residual variation that can be clustered within each class to infer codes suitable for exchange. The second hypothesizes that distilling ERM on original examples limits the source-accuracy loss to no more than 1 percentage point. Neither claim is an established result.
Why specify clustering within each class rather than just clustering residuals generally?

The within-class qualification is meant to keep the search for residual variation tied to examples sharing a label. Conceptually, that may make it easier to look for differences other than the class distinction itself. It does not guarantee that every difference within a class is nuisance variation, or that all label-relevant structure has left the residual.
And what role does the supervised bottleneck play before that clustering?

Its hypothesized role is to concentrate predictive structure in a representation shaped by the supervised task, so the remaining residual is a more promising place to look for nuisance variation. That describes the intended separation. It does not establish that the bottleneck retains every genuinely predictive feature or excludes every spurious cue.
Does calling something a residual mean it is safe to exchange?

No. A residual is defined by what remains after the bottleneck, not by an assurance that it lacks predictive information. The hypothesis is specifically that clustering those residuals within classes can isolate *exchangeable nuisance codes*. Exchangeability is the property that still needs to hold; it does not follow merely from using residuals.
Suppose spurious cues co-occur closely with genuine features. How does this hypothesis bear on that concern?

It proposes a way to separate their roles: preserve predictive structure through the supervised bottleneck, then look within classes for residual patterns to use as nuisance codes. But close co-occurrence is also why the hypothesis is uncertain. Genuine structure could remain in a residual cluster, and a spurious cue could be retained by the bottleneck. Either would complicate the intended interpretation of a swap.
So the clustering is not itself a demonstration that a code represents a nuisance?

Right. Clustering groups residual patterns; it does not determine whether those patterns are irrelevant to the prediction that should be preserved. The hypothesis adds that the resulting within-class groups isolate *exchangeable* nuisance codes, which is a stronger claim than simply obtaining clusters.
How does this connect to exchanging codes across labels in SwapAnchor?

The proposal would use the inferred nuisance codes as the components exchanged across labels. The hypothesis addresses the prerequisite for interpreting such exchanges: that the codes can be changed without carrying away genuinely predictive structure. It does not change the across-label nature of the proposed exchange or establish that every resulting counterfactual is valid.
I want to keep the second part precise. What does “limits source-accuracy loss to ≤1 point” mean here?

It is a hypothesized bound on an accuracy difference, expressed in percentage points. In the context of the goal, ERM is the reference for source accuracy: the claim is that distillation would keep a drop from ERM to no more than 1 percentage point. It is not a claim of a 1% relative change, and no measured source accuracy is being reported.
Is ERM distillation being asked to isolate the nuisance codes too?

Not in this hypothesis. Within-class residual clustering after supervised bottlenecking is the proposed route to isolating exchangeable nuisance codes. ERM distillation has the separate hypothesized role of limiting source-accuracy loss, consistent with its use on original examples in the SwapAnchor proposal. It does not, by itself, show that the residual codes are exchangeable.
Could the two parts pull in different directions?

Conceptually, they could. The code exchanges and consistency objective are intended to reduce sensitivity to nuisance variation, while distillation encourages retention of ERM-like behavior on original examples. The hypothesis is that this combination can preserve source accuracy while permitting meaningful nuisance exchanges; it does not settle how those pressures interact.
Does the hypothesis say how many clusters to use or how to construct the bottleneck?

No. It specifies the sequence and roles—supervised bottlenecking, then within-class residual clustering to infer exchangeable nuisance codes, alongside ERM distillation to limit source-accuracy loss—but not an architecture, cluster count, objective formula, or other implementation choice. Adding one would go beyond the stated hypothesis.
Does “within-class” assume source-domain annotations?

No. “Within-class” refers to the supervised class labels, not identifiers for source domains. As stated, the hypothesis does not require source-domain annotations or target-domain data. That distinction matters because the broader goal rules out relying on either of those sources of domain information.
Would meeting the one-point source-accuracy condition be enough to establish the whole domain-generalization goal?

No. Even if ERM distillation limited source-accuracy loss to at most 1 percentage point, the method would still need to preserve genuinely predictive features and achieve at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under unseen combinations of spurious correlations. The hypothesis addresses code exchangeability and source-accuracy retention; it does not report either accuracy outcome.
What's the key uncertainty about the first part, stated as plainly as possible?

Whether the supervised bottleneck leaves behind residual variation that can be clustered into codes representing nuisance information *without* also separating out genuinely predictive structure. If it does not, an across-label swap may not be a clean nuisance change, and consistency under that swap may be misleading.
Then how should I phrase the whole idea without making it sound proven?

One phrasing is: “We hypothesize that within-class clustering of residuals after supervised bottlenecking can isolate exchangeable nuisance codes for SwapAnchor, even when spurious cues co-occur with genuine features. We further hypothesize that distilling ERM on original examples limits the loss in source accuracy relative to ERM to no more than 1 percentage point.” That states both proposed mechanisms and their intended effects without presenting either as an observed result.

To investigate the exchangeability question, I plan to fit a supervised bottleneck, cluster the within-class residuals, swap the resulting codes across labels, and then audit causal-feature retention and source accuracy on ColorShape-Mix.

That gives the investigation a clear order. First fit the supervised bottleneck; then cluster residual variation within each class to obtain candidate codes; next exchange those codes across labels; finally audit whether the process retains causal features and what happens to source accuracy on ColorShape-Mix. These are planned steps, not findings about the codes or the method’s performance.
Why does the bottleneck come before the residual clustering?

The order reflects the proposed distinction between predictive structure and what remains after supervised bottlenecking. Clustering the residuals afterward asks whether that remaining variation can yield exchangeable nuisance codes. The sequence expresses the intended separation, but it does not establish that the bottleneck has captured all genuinely predictive information.
Is clustering within each class important to the plan?

Yes. The plan specifically calls for within-class residual clustering, not clustering all residuals without regard to class. That focuses the clustering on variation among examples with the same label. It still leaves open whether the resulting clusters represent nuisance variation rather than predictive structure that also varies within a class.
When do those clusters become codes for the swaps?

In the planned sequence, the within-class residual clustering supplies the candidate codes, and the next step is to swap codes across labels. Calling them candidate codes at that point is cautious: the later audit bears on whether treating them as exchangeable nuisance codes was warranted.
Why retain the across-label swap instead of treating the clustering as the endpoint?

Clustering alone would show only that residuals can be grouped. The planned swaps put the intended use of those groups into play: can the inferred component be exchanged across labels without stripping away the predictive structure that should remain? The exchange is therefore part of investigating the original question, not a conclusion supplied by the clustering step.
What exactly is the causal-feature-retention audit meant to guard against?

It is meant to guard against mistaking a damaged prediction problem for a clean nuisance intervention. If the bottleneck or the code exchange removes genuinely predictive structure, consistency after a swap would not have the intended interpretation. Auditing causal-feature retention asks whether the features that genuinely support prediction remain available through the planned process. The plan names that audit but does not specify its procedure or report its outcome.
Could a swap look successful even if that audit raises a concern?

Conceptually, yes. A model might give a stable prediction after an exchange because it has become insensitive to information it should have preserved. That is why the plan does not stop at swapping codes: it calls for an audit of causal-feature retention afterward. Stability under exchange and retention of predictive structure are distinct questions.
And what is the source-accuracy audit doing alongside it?

It checks the performance side of the preservation concern on the sources. A procedure that makes predictions less sensitive to swapped codes could also impair accuracy on original source examples. Auditing source accuracy alongside causal-feature retention keeps that possible cost visible; the plan itself does not say what the accuracy will be.
Are the two audits interchangeable?

No. Source accuracy concerns predictive performance on the sources, whereas causal-feature retention concerns whether genuinely predictive structure survives the proposed separation and swaps. Good source accuracy would not, by itself, prove that the inferred codes are clean nuisance codes; a retention check also does not replace an accuracy measurement.
What role does ColorShape-Mix have in the wording of the plan?

ColorShape-Mix is the named setting for the planned audits of causal-feature retention and source accuracy. The plan does not supply its composition, results, or audit procedure, so there is no basis here to describe those details or to infer what the audits will find.
Does this plan already answer whether SwapAnchor can infer exchangeable codes when spurious cues co-occur with genuine features?

No. It lays out a way to investigate that question. The bottleneck and within-class clustering propose where exchangeable codes might come from; the across-label swaps exercise that proposal; the audits address the risk of losing causal features or source accuracy. Whether the codes actually isolate nuisance variation remains open.
Should I describe the retention audit as occurring before the swaps, so I can certify the codes first?

That would change the stated sequence. Your plan says to fit the bottleneck, cluster within-class residuals, swap codes across labels, *then* audit causal-feature retention and source accuracy on ColorShape-Mix. The audit can examine the consequences of the planned procedure without implying that the codes were certified in advance.
I also want to avoid implying that fitting a supervised bottleneck requires domain labels.

The plan calls it a supervised bottleneck and separately specifies within-class clustering, which refers to class labels. It does not call for source-domain annotations or target-domain data. Nothing in the stated sequence requires describing the classes as domains.
Does the plan specify how to fit the bottleneck, form clusters, perform swaps, or run the audits?

No. It states the stages and their order, the across-label condition on the swaps, and the two audit subjects on ColorShape-Mix. It does not fix an architecture, clustering rule, swap construction, audit metric, or outcome. Those particulars should not be presented as though they are already part of this plan.
Can you state the plan plainly, keeping the investigation separate from its hoped-for result?

Fit a supervised bottleneck, cluster residuals within each class, exchange the inferred codes across labels, and then audit causal-feature retention and source accuracy on ColorShape-Mix. This is a planned test of whether the inferred codes can be used as exchangeable nuisance codes without stripping predictive structure; it does not assert that the test will succeed.
The activity is to train SwapAnchor using four within-class residual clusters, cross-label nuisance swaps, and ERM distillation, then score source and unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations.

That specifies the training ingredients and the settings to score. The four clusters come from within-class residuals; the inferred nuisance codes are swapped across labels; and ERM supplies the distillation reference. Source and unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations are both included in scoring. No accuracy values or conclusions about the swaps are stated yet.
Does “four within-class residual clusters” specify exactly how the clustering is done?

No. It fixes the number four and says the clusters concern residuals within classes. It does not specify a clustering algorithm, how residuals are represented, or further details of cluster construction.
Should we call the resulting codes confirmed nuisance codes at this point?

Not merely because they came from those clusters. “Nuisance” describes their intended role in SwapAnchor, and the activity uses them for cross-label swaps. Whether they isolate exchangeable nuisance information without carrying genuinely predictive structure is still a question, not an outcome established by the training description.
Why keep “cross-label” explicit?

It distinguishes the specified swaps from exchanging codes only among examples with the same label. The activity calls for nuisance-code exchanges across labels. That detail matters to what SwapAnchor is being asked to handle, though it does not by itself guarantee that an exchanged example preserves its original predictive structure.
Is ERM distillation a separate part of training from the swaps?

Yes. Both are named training ingredients, but they serve different intended roles. The swaps expose SwapAnchor to changes in the inferred nuisance codes, while ERM distillation provides a reference for predictive behavior on original examples. The activity does not specify their relative strength or report how they interact.
Does using four clusters mean we have solved the problem of separating spurious cues from genuine features?

No. Four is a concrete choice for this activity, not evidence that the residuals divide cleanly into nuisance and genuinely predictive information. The earlier concern still applies: if a cluster carries predictive structure, swapping its code could disturb more than a nuisance cue.
What exactly should be scored after training?

The activity names two scoring settings: the sources and unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations. It does not give scores, specify which combinations are included, or define a new metric beyond the accuracy comparisons in the broader goal.
Why score the sources as well as the unseen combinations?

They address different parts of the intended performance picture. Source scoring makes any loss of accuracy there visible; scoring unseen combinations addresses behavior where familiar associations may not carry over in the same way. Including both prevents the activity from looking only at generalization or only at source performance.
Can we already say the source score is within one percentage point of ERM?

No. ERM distillation is part of training, but the activity provides no measured source score. The within-one-percentage-point condition is a requirement to check, not a consequence we can declare from the presence of distillation.
What about the target of at least five percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM?

That remains the broader performance target under unseen combinations of spurious correlations. Scoring unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations can provide information relevant to it, but this activity states no worst-domain accuracy, ERM comparison result, or achieved improvement.
Does scoring unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations mean SwapAnchor used data from them during training?

No. Scoring a trained method on unseen combinations is distinct from supplying those combinations as target-domain data to train it. The activity says to score them; it does not say to use their data to infer codes, perform swaps, or distill ERM during training.
And does within-class clustering require source-domain annotations?
Not as stated. “Within-class” refers to class labels, whereas source-domain annotations identify domains. The activity specifies the former and does not add a requirement for domain identifiers.
Should the source and unseen scores be presented as evidence that the codes are exchangeable?

They would be performance observations once measured, but scores alone would not necessarily show what each code contains. In particular, they would not by themselves establish that a swap changes only nuisance information while retaining every genuinely predictive feature. The activity here specifies training and scoring, not such a conclusion.
Does this activity include a reported causal-feature-retention audit?

No audit result is reported here. The specified activity is to train SwapAnchor with the four within-class residual clusters, cross-label nuisance swaps, and ERM distillation, and to score the sources and unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations. It should not be worded as though causal-feature retention has already been demonstrated.
How much implementation detail can we infer from this description?

Only the stated choices. It does not fix the bottleneck architecture, clustering algorithm, code format, swap construction, distillation formula, or scoring results. Supplying any of those as a settled part of the activity would go beyond what has been specified.
Then give me a precise description that doesn't turn the activity into a result.

Train SwapAnchor with four within-class residual clusters, cross-label nuisance-code swaps, and ERM distillation; score accuracy on the sources and on unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations. This describes what is being done and evaluated, without asserting that the codes are exchangeable or that either performance target has been met.
What does the ColorShape-Mix v1 report contain?
It contains SwapAnchor and ERM checkpoints, inferred nuisance-cluster assignments, causal-feature probes, and accuracy tables for source and unseen ColorShape-Mix combinations.
Are the checkpoints included for both models?
Yes. The inventory explicitly names both SwapAnchor and ERM checkpoints. It does not specify their file formats or any other checkpoint details.
What should I understand by “inferred nuisance-cluster assignments”?

They are the report’s record of assignments to inferred nuisance clusters. The description does not reproduce the assignments or say how they are displayed. “Inferred” is worth retaining: the inventory does not describe them as supplied nuisance labels.
Does the report description give the individual cluster assignments?
No individual assignments are listed in the description you provided. It says that the ColorShape-Mix v1 report contains them.
How should I refer to the causal-feature probes without filling in their results?
Call them “causal-feature probes.” That accurately identifies another component of the report without specifying probe procedures, readings, or findings that are not included in this inventory.
Are the accuracy tables only for the sources?
No. The report contains source and unseen accuracy tables, covering both settings. The description does not give their entries or layout.
Does “unseen” identify the exact combinations tabulated?
Not here. It identifies the unseen side of the accuracy tables, but the inventory does not list particular ColorShape-Mix combinations.
Can I quote any accuracy numbers from this node?
No numbers are supplied in the report description. It says accuracy tables are present, but their entries are not reproduced here.
Is “v1” part of the report’s name?
Yes. “ColorShape-Mix v1 report” is the named artifact. There is no need to infer anything about other versions from that name.
Could you separate the contents into model artifacts and the other report components?
